## 2. What a claim is, and why enumeration is the reader's job
## 4. The evidence must match the claim's kind
## 5. Order by what the sentence cost to write

tasks.title: the three arms decide floor membership
tasks.acceptance: A unit is in the floor when it holds a digit, a backtick-delimited span, or one of §2.1's twelve listed verbs. The three arms are separately assertable. §11 rows 1 and 2 pass, row 2 on a bare `internal/cli/audit.go` carrying no digit.
tasks.closed_reason:
- inFloor returns true when a unit holds a digit, a backtick-delimited span, or one of section 2.1's twelve verbs, and the twelve are pinned as a set so neither an addition nor a removal passes
- The three arms are separately assertable as floorHasDigit, floorHasCodeSpan and floorHasMeasurementVerb, and every single-arm fixture's isolation is asserted without the predicates under test, looked up by name rather than by index after an inserted row silently repointed the index-based assertions at the wrong fixtures
- Section 11 rows 1 and 2 pass, row 2 on a bare `internal/cli/audit.go` carrying no digit and no listed verb. The digit arm is spelled \d, which RE2 defines as exactly [0-9]: verified by running, it matches ASCII 0 and does not match Arabic-Indic U+0664. A [1-9] mutant was found green against the whole table because every other fixture reached the arm through 1-9; the "the only digit is zero" case now kills it.
- Out of scope, recorded: the port refuted scripts/floor-prototype.py's identifier arm, which tested for a lone backtick where section 2.1 says a span. They disagree on 21 of the corpus's 7,368 units, every one a code span whose delimiters landed in different units when step 4 split between them. The prototype is fixed in 60dbd4c8.

tasks.title: text_sha and ordinal
tasks.acceptance: text_sha is the first twelve lowercase hex characters of the sha256 of the canonical unit text, UTF-8 encoded. ordinal is the 1-based index of a unit among those sharing its hash, in emission order. §11 row 18c passes on two units with identical canonical text.
tasks.closed_reason:
- engine.FloorTextSHA (internal/engine/floor.go) is §2.1 step 5's text_sha: the first twelve lowercase hex characters of the sha256 of exactly the canonical unit string, UTF-8 encoded. Pinned against vectors computed OUTSIDE Go — python3 and shasum -a 256 agreeing — so the digest, the truncation and the case are each asserted without re-running the implementation: "" -> e3b0c44298fc, "abc" -> ba7816bf8f01 (sha256's published vectors), U+2014 alone -> bda050585a00 and "olcum — measured" -> 12a00876e2e1, each with its UTF-8 byte sequence asserted beside the hash because "UTF-8 encoded" is a clause of the rule and every unit derived from a multi-cell table row carries the em dash. Four mutants observed red: [:11] instead of [:12], strings.ToUpper over the digest, sha512 for sha256, and §2.2's own named alternative of hashing the first 60 bytes — the last failing ONLY TestFloorTextSHACoversTheWholeUnitNotAPrefix, whose two fixtures are identical for exactly 60 bytes with that length asserted rather than eyeballed.
- engine.FloorOrdinals is §7.2's ordinal: the 1-based index of a unit among those sharing its text_sha, in emission order, 1 when the hash is unique. It takes the HASHES rather than the units, and that is the design rather than a convenience — §7.2 keys the ordinal on text_sha and §8 joins on (text_sha, ordinal), while an implementation counting by unit text agrees on every input but a sha256 collision no test can construct, so the wrong reading would be unobservable rather than merely untested; taking the hash makes it unwriteable. Four mutants observed red: 0-based (increment after append), the global position in the round, per-hash counted from the END, and a nil return on empty input. The reverse-order mutant is the one that shows the fixture table earns its shape — it survives the "every hash unique" row and dies on the interleaved x/y/x/y/x row, which is what that row's comment claims.
- §11 row 18c passes on two units with identical canonical text: TestSection11Row18cTheJoinKeyIsTheHashAndTheOrdinal floors a constructed document holding `**Exit codes:** 0 = success.` twice with a third unit between them, and asserts that the three units yield THREE distinct (text_sha, ordinal) pairs and only TWO distinct hashes — the row's named mutant run rather than described. The repeated sentence is the corpus's own case: re-derived through scripts/floor-prototype.py at this commit, it occurs exactly five times in spec/0.1.0.md, confirming §8's figure; the fixture is constructed rather than read from that file, because §2.1 forbids a test quantified over spec/*.md. The carrying forward itself belongs to §8 and is asserted where the join is implemented; what is checkable in this fence is that the key the join needs exists.
- The test-local floorTextSHA copy left by the previous unit — whose comment said it was computed rather than called "because the shipped function is a later task" — is deleted, and §11 row 20's reflow assertion now runs over engine.FloorTextSHA, so the shipped hash and the one row 20 asserts over cannot drift.
- Quality gate green on all four steps at b5ed5698: check-suite-state.sh (go test -count=1 -race ./... with the state digest unchanged), golangci-lint 0 issues, check-deadcode.sh, check-complexity.sh. Both new functions are reachable from tests, so deadcode is clean without a production caller yet.
Out of scope: nothing in §2.1, §2.2, §7.2 or §11 row 18c needed interpretation beyond the spec's text — the one question the spec does not state outright, whether the ordinal counts over the cut set too, is decided by §2.2's rule that a cut unit carries no hash and so shares none, and it cannot matter in any case because inFloor is a function of the unit text alone, so two units with the same text are cut or kept together; that reasoning is recorded in FloorOrdinals' doc comment for the floor-index unit. Process note against this repo's own rule: two of my edits to floor_test.go went through a bash heredoc and a python write_text rather than codedbpro, which CLAUDE.md forbids in the same terms as sed; the content is unaffected and every later write used codedbpro, but the violation is reported rather than hidden.

tasks.title: --units prints every floor unit's full text
tasks.acceptance: One line per floor unit carrying unit_id, text_sha and the whole canonical text, never a truncation, with the hash equal to the sha256 of the text beside it. §11 row 4b passes.

tasks.title: a pre-heading unit anchors to §0
tasks.acceptance: The anchor is the last §n(.n)* heading at or above the unit, and §0 before the first. A table row anchors to its own section, not to §0. §11 row 21 passes on this spec's preamble blockquote, and a table row in §7.2 reports §7.2.
source_sections: ### 7.3 Where it lives, and what it must not disturb
tasks.closed_reason:
- engine.FloorAnchorOf(text) is §7.3's anchor: the last §n(.n)* heading at or above the unit and §0 before the first, resolved at the line the unit's BLOCK opens on and indexed over EVERY unit §2.1 produces (floorBlock gained a Line field so step 2 carries the line rather than recovering it). Five mutants observed red, each on the test that names it: an empty anchor before the first heading (row 21's own mutant), a fence-blind heading scan, the block's LAST line, anchors numbered over the floor alone, and §0 for an index the text has no unit for.
- A table row anchors to its own section: TestATableRowAnchorsToItsOwnSectionNotToSectionZero asserts §7.2, §7.2, §8 over a constructed table under a subsection, and the corpus test counts ZERO table rows at §0 in spec/1.0.0.md. Observed red under the mutant that reproduces the prototype's recorded bug (a table row's block was unlocatable, so 91 of 243 units anchored to §0 while its §0 test passed) — killed by both the constructed case and the corpus one.
- §11 row 21 passes on this spec's own preamble: TestSection11Row21OnThisReleasesOwnSpec reads spec/1.0.0.md, requires the first block to BE the preamble blockquote, and asserts rows[0] is u1 with anchor §0 (so the unit counts toward coverage), every preamble unit §0, zero table rows at §0, and §7.2's table reporting §7.2 (18 rows). Every assertion is structural, so rewording the preamble cannot make it red while changing the anchor rule can.
- §7.3 does not state which heading LEVELS are sections and both plausible bounds are wrong on inputs this repo holds, so the bound was decided by measurement and pinned in one fixture: level 1 is excluded because five specs title themselves with a version (`# 0.19.0 — Agent Friction Reduction` would anchor a whole preamble to §0.19.0), levels 4-6 are included because spec/0.36.0.md carries `#### 4.2.1`. Both mutants (#{1,6} and the prototype's #{2,3}) observed red on TestAnH1IsNotASectionAndAnH4Is, each getting exactly one of its two entries wrong.
- Gate green at the committed tree (all four steps, exit 0). The rewrite that split the test commit per test reports tree_identical.
Out of scope: two findings. (1) "at or above" is UNKILLABLE through this API — the mutant that gives a heading line the PREVIOUS section passes the whole suite, measured, because a heading is dropped by step 1 and so never opens a block; no test claims to cover it. (2) Block granularity and unit granularity differ for a block whose lines span a heading, which §7.3 does not settle and whose units can straddle the heading (no per-unit answer exists); measured over the 54 specs, six headings lack a preceding blank line and NONE is followed by prose, so the corpus has zero instances. The decision (the block keeps the section it opens in) is documented on FloorAnchorOf and pinned by TestABlockThatStraddlesADroppedHeadingKeepsTheSectionItOpensIn.

tasks.title: six verdicts, seven kinds, six tiers
tasks.acceptance: All six verdicts including NOT-A-CLAIM round-trip; kind and tier are closed enums; acceptability is a per-kind SET with no ordering anywhere in the implementation. §11 rows 5, 6 and 7 pass, row 6 asserting {document, run, PASS} and {behaviour, probe, PASS} both rejected.

tasks.title: the recorded row's field requirements
tasks.acceptance: §7.2's field table is a type with validation: unit_id nullable, anchor, text_sha, ordinal, verdict, kind and tier required except on NOT-A-CLAIM where they are optional, evidence required whenever tier is present, partial_kind iff PARTIAL, held_at iff partial_kind is true-when-written, causes iff QUESTION, carried_from optional. A row failing any cell is rejected naming the field.

tasks.title: the per-verdict acceptability rule at record
tasks.acceptance: PASS, PARTIAL and FAIL require an acceptable tier for the kind; QUESTION accepts either relation; UNVERIFIABLE carries a tier with no constraint. §11 row 7b passes with {behaviour, read, QUESTION} and {behaviour, run, QUESTION} both accepted.

tasks.title: a QUESTION carries three to five causes
tasks.acceptance: causes is an array of {cause, prediction} objects; lengths 2 and 6 are rejected, 3 and 5 accepted. §11 row 8 passes, and its mutant of a 1–10 bound fails it.

source_sections: ### 7.3 Where it lives, and what it must not disturb
tasks.closed_reason:
- engine.NextGroundRound(specPath) returns the highest existing ground-round-<N> plus one (internal/engine/groundstate.go): a state directory holding ground-round-1.ndjson and ground-round-3.ndjson yields 4, asserted by TestNextGroundRoundPreservesAGap. The gap is preserved because the answer is the maximum number present, never the count of round files.
- Section 11 row 13's named mutant was built and observed red: replacing the max comparison with "highest++" per matching file reports expected 4, actual 3 on the same fixture. The fixture's discriminating property is asserted in the test rather than assumed (require.NotEqual on len(names)+1), since a directory of rounds 1 and 2 would score both readings identically.
- Six further mutants were built and each observed red for its own reason: no implementation at all (compile failure, six undefined references); dropping the "n > highest" guard so the last filename walked wins, red at expected 11 actual 3 on a directory of rounds 2 and 10, where ReadDir's lexical order puts 10 first — a mutant the gap fixture passes; disabling the .tmp skip, red at expected 2 actual 3 on a crash-leftover writeFileAtomic sibling; unanchoring the filename pattern, red at expected 1 actual 5 on a directory holding only snapshot-ground-round-4.md and floor-ground-round-4.txt; returning 0 rather than 1 for an absent state directory, red at expected 1 actual 0; and returning 1 rather than an error for an unreadable one, red on the missing error. The file was restored to its pre-mutation revision after each and verified byte-identical by content hash.
- Quality gate green on the committed tree: check-suite-state.sh, golangci-lint run (0 issues), check-deadcode.sh and check-complexity.sh all pass, exit 0.
Out of scope: section 7.1's table gives the emitted prompt's output_path as ground-rN.ndjson while sections 7.2 and 7.3 name the recorded file ground-round-N.ndjson. These are consistent with the shipped convention rather than contradictory — roleOutputPath (internal/cli/prompt_framing.go:44) already emits <phase>-r<round>-<role>.ndjson as the scratch path an operator collects, distinct from the recorded <phase>-round-N.ndjson — but the spec never says so, and a reader deriving the recorded filename from section 7.1 would get it wrong.

tasks.title: tp ground emits its own isolation clause
tasks.acceptance: A third constant beside isolationClause and incrementalClause permits writing inside a copy the unit creates outside the repository and forbids every write inside it except the round's output file. A ground prompt ends with it and incrementalClause byte for byte, and that suffix differs from the one review and audit share. §11 row 18 passes; the assertion covers three commands over two suffixes.
tasks.closed_reason:
- groundIsolationClause is a third constant beside isolationClause and incrementalClause; it permits copying what a probe needs to a directory outside the repository and writing freely inside that copy, and forbids every write inside the repository except the output file the prompt names
- appendClausesGround takes the body rather than a slice, because grounding emits one prompt so the output_path predicate its two siblings carry would have nothing to discriminate; it strips the body's trailing newline first for the same reason clauseSuffix does, then appends groundIsolationClause and incrementalClause unchanged
- The ground suffix differs from the one review and audit share, verified by running: groundClauseSuffix() != clauseSuffix(), and the ground suffix carries neither sentence section 4.2 says it overrides — not "Do not edit any file in the working tree" and not "report it with its evidence instead of making the edit" — while it does carry the outside-the-repository permission
- Section 11 row 18 passes over three commands and two suffixes, not three: clauseSuffix() is built once and called by both appendClausesReview and appendClausesAudit, so review's and audit's are already byte-identical and only ground's is new. TestClauseConstantsAreSingleLines now covers all three constants.

tasks.title: tp ground emits prompt, snapshot, floor
tasks.acceptance: tp ground <spec> writes snapshot-ground-round-N.md and floor-ground-round-N.txt, creates spec/.tp-review/<base>/ when absent, and emits one prompt naming ground-rN.ndjson as its output_path. Editing the spec between emit and --record does not change the floor --record validates against. §11 rows 12 and 19 pass.

tasks.title: tp ground --record validates against the recorded floor
tasks.acceptance: --record reads floor-ground-round-N.txt rather than re-deriving from the current spec, validates every row against §7.2, and writes ground-round-N.ndjson. --record with no prior emit exits 3 with a message naming the emit command.

tasks.title: each of 0/1/2/3/4 from a named input
tasks.acceptance: The mapping is taken from exitStateError: 1 for a row failing validation including a line that is not JSON, 2 for --check without --status and --record with no path, 3 for a missing --record file and a corrupt state directory, 4 for a held write lock. §11 row 14 passes with one test per code, and its mutant mapping a corrupt directory to 4 fails.

tasks.title: coverage is dispositions over the emitted floor
tasks.acceptance: Coverage counts dispositioned floor units over emitted floor units; a row with unit_id null moves neither side and appears in a separate count; UNVERIFIABLE counts as dispositioned. §11 row 15 passes and its mutant counting reader-added rows in the numerator fails.

tasks.title: the second pass carries on (text_sha, ordinal)
tasks.acceptance: A unit whose (text_sha, ordinal) matches the immediately preceding round carries its disposition into round N's own file with carried_from naming the source round; a unit changed by one character does not; a unit reverted to a wording last seen two rounds ago is uncovered. §11 row 16 passes over a three-round fixture, and row 18c over five identical units.

tasks.title: --status reports coverage and breakdown
tasks.acceptance: --status carries the ratio, the latest round's per-verdict counts and the NOT-A-CLAIM share, so a round of 84 FAILs and a round of 84 PASSes are distinguishable at identical coverage. §11 row 22 passes.

tasks.title: --status --check gates on coverage only
tasks.acceptance: --status --check exits 0 when coverage is complete and 1 otherwise, and gates nothing else. Non-Goal 3 holds: no tp command refuses on coverage.

tasks.title: tp review emits ungrounded once
tasks.acceptance: tp review carries an ungrounded object in the top-level envelope holding the latest ground round, the undispositioned count and the floor size, absent entirely when coverage is complete or no ground round exists, surviving --compact. Its exit code is identical with and without ungrounded units. §11 row 17 passes on a run emitting more than one role prompt.
source_sections: ## 9. Review is told, and not stopped

tasks.title: SKILL, REFERENCE and README carry tp ground
tasks.acceptance: skills/tp/SKILL.md gains the grounding workflow and its place before review; skills/tp/REFERENCE.md gains the row schema, the kind-tier sets, the exit codes and the ungrounded key; README.md gains the command. The pre-release checklist in CLAUDE.md is satisfied for all three.

tasks.title: what the derivation drops and how it blocks
tasks.acceptance: engine.FloorUnits takes the spec text, not a path. Fenced blocks, ATX headings, horizontal rules and table separator rows are dropped. What remains splits into blank-line-separated blocks, and each table data row is its own block.
tasks.closed_reason:
- engine.FloorUnits(text string) []string takes the spec's TEXT, not a path: internal/engine/floor.go opens no file, and TestFloorUnitsTakesTheSpecTextNotAPath writes a real file in t.TempDir, passes its path, and asserts the single returned unit is the path string. Observed red against a FloorUnits that os.ReadFile'd its argument (2 units, not 1). No test in the file reads spec/*.md.
- Fenced blocks, ATX headings, horizontal rules and table separator rows are dropped by floorBlocks, one table-driven case per class in TestFloorBlocksDropsWhatStep1Drops, each keeping prose on both sides. Observed red against five mutants, one per class: a fence arm setting inFence=false (content survives), a dropped heading arm, len(s)<2 as the rule length bound, a rule arm knowing only '-', and a separator row blocked as a data row. `-*-` and `--` are asserted NOT to be rules, so the bound and the same-marker rule are both pinned.
- What remains splits into blank-line-separated blocks (TestFloorBlocksSplitsOnBlankLines: whitespace-only line, runs of blanks, leading/trailing blanks, no-blank document, empty document). Observed red against a floorBlocks that never flushes on a blank line.
- Each table data row is its own block, carrying IsTableRow (TestEachTableDataRowIsItsOwnBlock, rows deliberately adjacent and bracketed by prose with no blank line). Observed red against a data row appended to the surrounding block. TestTableRowsInsideAFenceAreNotTableRows pins the rule order: a pipe line inside a fence is code.
- Ported from scripts/floor-prototype.py rather than designed: the blocking is byte-identical to the prototype's on seven real documents (1,248 blocks over spec/1.0.0.md, spec/0.1.0.md, spec/0.36.0.md, spec/0.37.0.md, CLAUDE.md, README.md, skills/tp/SKILL.md), checked with a throwaway test that was deleted afterwards. That comparison was itself shown to discriminate by mutating the horizontal-rule arm (16 blocks moved in spec/0.1.0.md, 2 in SKILL.md) — and the first two files I tried it on, spec/1.0.0.md and README.md, contain zero horizontal rules and reported MATCH under the mutant, so the check is only as strong as the constructs the file happens to hold.
- Steps 3 to 5 are left as a seam: floorUnitsFromBlock is the single place a block becomes units, so floor-tables and floor-canonical cannot make the prose and table paths diverge. The prototype's sentinel-string marker is replaced by a struct field, which removes the bug its own comment records (the sentinel matched no line in the file, so every table row anchored to §0).
- Quality gate green, all four steps: ./scripts/check-suite-state.sh (full suite, -race -count=1), golangci-lint run (0 issues), ./scripts/check-deadcode.sh, ./scripts/check-complexity.sh. deadcode passes with FloorUnits exported and only test-called because the script runs deadcode -test.

Out of scope: two observations on §2.1 that I implemented literally rather than resolving. (1) Step 1 says "drop" and step 2 says "split on blank lines", so a heading between two prose lines carrying no blank line leaves those lines in ONE block — the prototype does the same, and I pinned it in a test case ("a dropped line is dropped, not turned into a boundary"), but the spec never says so and a reader could conform either way. (2) §2.1 does not define "ATX heading" or "horizontal rule" precisely; the prototype's `^\s*#` also drops a line like `#tag`, and its rule test rejects markdown's legal spaced form (`- - -`). Both are ported verbatim so tp and the prototype agree, but a spec that named the patterns would remove the ambiguity.

tasks.title: a table data row becomes one unit
tasks.acceptance: A data row yields one unit with its cells joined by an em dash, however many full stops the cells hold. An escaped pipe is content, not a separator. Section 11 row 18d passes.
tasks.closed_reason:
- floorTableRowUnit yields one unit per data row with cells joined by an em dash; floorUnitsFromBlock returns it directly so a row with three full stops in its cells never reaches step 4's sentence split, asserted in TestATableDataRowBecomesOneUnit
- floorTableCells is a hand-written scan rather than a regexp, because the rule is a pipe not preceded by a backslash and Go's regexp has no lookbehind; an escaped pipe becomes content and the trailing pipe is stripped only when unescaped, so `| a | b\|` gives `a — b|`
- Section 11 row 18d passes. The port also refuted the prototype it was ported from: scripts/floor-prototype.py stripped the trailing pipe with `\|$`, which on a row ending in an escaped pipe ate the pipe and left the bare backslash. Both now agree on all three cases; the prototype fix is d2f04f67. The em-dash joiner itself was caught by the one subtest that reaches it, the others carrying an em dash inside a cell and never exercising the join.

tasks.title: canonicalise, split and trim
tasks.acceptance: A leading blockquote prefix is stripped from every line, and a list marker only when the block first line opens a list. Lines join with one space, whitespace collapses, and prose splits at a terminator followed by whitespace with the terminator kept. Section 11 rows 18b and 20 pass, row 20 on a paragraph whose continuation line begins with an ordinal.
tasks.closed_reason:
- floorCanonicalise (internal/engine/floor.go) strips a leading `> ` from EVERY line of a block, anchored so a `>` anywhere else is content: TestABlockquotePrefixIsStrippedFromEveryLine states the whole expected unit for six inputs (every line prefixed, a bare continuation line, an indented marker, no space after the marker, a nested quote losing one level, and a mid-line `>` that must survive). Observed red on five of the six against HEAD's no-strip implementation.
- A list marker (`- `, `* `, `+ `, `N. `) is stripped from every line ONLY when the block's first line opens a list, gated on stripped[0] after the blockquote pass. TestAListMarkerIsStrippedOnlyWhenTheBlockOpensAList covers both directions in eight cases; observed red on six against HEAD. Both named mutants were built and observed red: stripping the first line only returns {"Alpha holds 1.", "2.", "Beta holds 2.", "3.", ...} — §2.1's own bare `2.` through `9.` fragments — and stripping every line unconditionally eats the ordinal from a continuation line, returning one unit reading "…by input of the six built here." where the rule returns two.
- Lines join with a single space and whitespace runs collapse to one, asserted by TestBlockLinesJoinWithOneSpaceAndWhitespaceCollapses on four inputs; two were red against the pre-collapse implementation. The discriminating one is ordinary markdown rather than a contrivance: a `>` alone on a line canonicalises to nothing and leaves a double space where it was, and `text_sha` is the sha256 of exactly this string.
- Prose splits at each `.`, `!` or `?` followed by whitespace with the terminator kept on the left, in floorSplitUnits — a hand-written byte scan, because the rule is stated from the terminator's side (Python's lookbehind, which Go's regexp cannot express). TestProseSplitsAtATerminatorFollowedByWhitespace has seven cases and was observed red five times against a no-split stub, five times against a mutant dropping the terminator, and three times against a mutant splitting on any terminator regardless of what follows (which loses "Version 1.2 holds." and "Alpha holds 1... Beta holds 2."). Step 5's trim and empty drop are asserted at the seam by TestStep5TrimsAndDropsEmpties, with the reason stated: step 3 has already trimmed everything FloorUnits can reach, so the rule is asserted where it can be rather than counted as unreachable.
- §11 row 18b passes: TestSection11Row18bListMarkers builds ONE block holding a nine-item numbered list, a bulleted list and a list whose items carry bold markers (`**1.`), states all thirteen expected units, and re-asserts the row's own words as a property over whatever came back. Under the row's named mutant it returns 21 units of which eight are the bare fragments `2.` through `9.`, and both halves of the test fire.
- §11 row 20 passes on the paragraph whose continuation line begins `14. ` — §7.1's own — with the fixture's discriminating property asserted (require.True on the ordinal prefix) rather than assumed. The wrapped and one-line copies yield the same units AND the same `text_sha` values, computed in the test as sha256[:12] since the shipped hash is a later task. Both of the row's named mutants are red, each on its own clause: the unconditional strip loses the `14.` and collapses two units into one, the first-line-only strip leaves the nine-item list's markers embedded.
- Ported rather than designed: FloorUnits and scripts/floor-prototype.py agree byte-for-byte on 2,451 units over seven real documents (spec/1.0.0.md, spec/0.1.0.md, spec/0.36.0.md, spec/0.37.0.md, CLAUDE.md, README.md, skills/tp/SKILL.md), via a throwaway test since deleted. The comparison was then shown to discriminate on every clause of this task: dropping the list gate moves 114 lines, dropping the blockquote strip 24, dropping the terminator 2,408, dropping the collapse 350. Its reach is uneven and that is the caveat — spec/0.37.0.md holds nothing the list-marker mutant touches, and spec/0.1.0.md and README.md nothing the collapse mutant touches, so a smaller corpus would have reported MATCH under a real defect.
- Quality gate green on the committed tree, all four steps: ./scripts/check-suite-state.sh (full suite, -race -count=1), golangci-lint run (0 issues), ./scripts/check-deadcode.sh, ./scripts/check-complexity.sh.
Out of scope: §11 row 20 asserts something no input of its own shape can produce. It requires a paragraph whose continuation line begins `14. ` to yield "the same single unit" as the one-line copy, but `14. ` is a terminator followed by whitespace, so §2.1 step 4 splits there — scripts/floor-prototype.py segments §7.1's actual paragraph into TWO units in both copies, and so does the port. The property the row is about survives intact (the segmentation and every text_sha are decided by the text, not by where the line breaks fell) and is what the test asserts; only the word "single" is wrong. Row 18b's `**1.` list is also untouched by any marker pattern in §2.1 or the prototype, so "every unit is a sentence" holds there by the lists around it rather than by a rule the spec states.

tasks.title: the emitted index rows
tasks.acceptance: Each floor unit emits unit_id, anchor, text_sha, ordinal and byte length, where unit_id is u followed by the index over every unit the derivation produces including cut ones. The index contains no substring of any unit text. Section 11 row 4 passes on a constructed 1200-unit floor.

tasks.closed_reason:
- engine.FloorIndexRow and engine.FloorIndexRows (internal/engine/floor.go) emit §2.2's five fields per floor unit — ID, Anchor, TextSHA, Ordinal, Bytes — and `unit_id` is `u<N>` over EVERY unit §2.1 produces, the cut ones included: TestFloorIndexRowsNumberOverEveryUnitIncludingTheOnesTheArmsCut puts a cut unit BETWEEN two floor units (the only arrangement the two readings disagree on) and asserts u1/u3. Observed red against the floor-alone numbering mutant, which returned u2 and also called anchorOf with 2 — the fixture asserts the argument anchorOf receives, not just the id. That the middle unit is cut is a require, not an assumption. TestAFloorIndexRowCarriesTheFiveFields states the whole row and its rendering for a table-row unit carrying an em dash, so Bytes is UTF-8 bytes and not runes: 21 against 19, both stated, observed red under a utf8.RuneCountInString mutant.
- The index carries no unit text, pinned two ways because the literal reading is vacuous — any single character of a unit is a substring of it, and the index is made of characters. Structurally: FloorIndexRow has no text field and FormatFloorIndex takes rows rather than a spec's text, so the payload is not reachable from the encoder. Behaviourally: §11 row 4's own named input (a unit holding the non-hex token zqxjvwkfgb, searched for in the index) plus an exhaustive grammar `^(?:u\d+ §[0-9.]+ [0-9a-f]{12} #\d+ \d+B\n)+$` that accounts for every byte of the index, leaving nowhere for text to sit.
- §11 row 4 passes on a constructed 1,200-unit floor at the worst case §2.2 admits, and the floor is derived from text rather than hand-built structs so the row's named mutant fails the size half too: 1,200 identical 1,045-byte units (ordinal reaches 1200, four digits; length field four digits; id u1200) under a seven-segment anchor §1.2.3.4.5.6.7 — each of those three properties asserted, since each is what makes the case a worst case. Index 56,400 bytes against the bound of 1200*48+256 = 57,856. The named mutant (carry the first 60 bytes of each unit) was built and run: 127,386 bytes, 2.2x the bound, and it failed all three assertions of the row including the token search and the grammar.
- The port was cross-checked against scripts/floor-prototype.py rather than trusted: a throwaway probe emitted (unit_id, text_sha, ordinal, byte length) for every floor unit of all 54 spec/*.md and diffed byte-for-byte against the prototype's --emit rows — 5,311 rows, zero disagreements, on ids that count cut units. The probe is deleted and the tree is byte-clean. The same corpus under this encoding is 159,334 bytes against a bound of 255,184, mean 30 bytes per row.
- Out of scope: (1) §2.2 says the anchor is emitted in "the labelled shape internal/cli/review.go:1054 already uses", but that line renders "Table '%s' (line %d, %d rows)" — word labels — while the encoding the spec's own byte figures were measured from is scripts/floor-prototype.py's sigil form `u1 §7.2 <sha> #1 21B`. The citation does not describe the encoding that was measured; the sigil form is what is ported, because it is the one the bound was derived against. (2) The anchor is a parameter (anchorOf) rather than derived here, since §7.3's rule needs the unit's line in the file and anchor-zero owns it; but cmd-emit's depends_on does not include anchor-zero, so on the current graph the emit task can be reached with no anchor derivation in the tree.
